title: Acids and Bases
seo_title: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Acids and Bases Worksheets (CAPS)
standard_code: Grade 11 Physical Sciences: Acids and bases
standard_text: The Arrhenius and Lowry–Brønsted theories of acids and bases; conjugate acid–base pairs; ampholytes; acid–base indicators; neutralisation reactions of acids with metal hydroxides, metal oxides and metal carbonates; writing equations for acid–base reactions. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 11, Chemistry: Acids and bases)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): Arrhenius and Lowry–Brønsted acids and bases, conjugate pairs, ampholytes, indicators and neutralisation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A Lowry–Brønsted acid donates a proton (H⁺).
body_html:
How to think about it

Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions in water; a base produces OH⁻ ions. Lowry–Brønsted: an acid is a proton donor and a base is a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, it becomes its conjugate base: HCl and Cl⁻ are a conjugate pair. An ampholyte, such as water, can act as an acid or a base.

Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water; acid + metal oxide → salt + water; acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Indicators change colour with pH: litmus, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and bromothymol blue.

Example

Conjugate base of H₂SO₄?

Remove one H⁺

Answer: HSO₄⁻

Example

HCl + NaOH → ?

Acid + base

Answer: NaCl + H₂O

Common mistakes

  • Removing an H atom with its electron for the conjugate base.
  • Thinking all bases dissolve in water (alkalis do).
  • Forgetting CO₂ when an acid reacts with a carbonate.

faq.q: Why is water called an ampholyte?
faq.a: It can donate a proton (forming OH⁻) or accept one (forming H₃O⁺).
